rv.q: We first meet Brian as a young man in his father’s record shop, replacing Bruch’s violin concerto with Elvis’s Hound Dog.
Whatever the truth, Wright’s interpretation makes for compelling theatre.
Kiln artistic director Amit Sharma’s staging is fluent and funny, deftly showing the seismic social changes rippling through Lennon and Epstein’s relationship.
I can’t say any of it ever quite resembles human interaction as we know it either.
It all feels both superficial and artificial: a fantasia of music history that could hardly feel much further from rock’n’roll.
For all that, PLEASE PLEASE ME certainly parades a good deal of heart and effort, wrapped neatly in a compelling dose of nostalgia.
Please Please Me is a thoughtful look at a tortured man who deserved much more than the world gave him.
But rights issues mean there is no music, and the structure reduces every scene to an incident rather than a drama.
Please Please Me is still a beautiful work of bittersweet whimsy.
There’s a lot of fun and joy in this story but the play can’t find it because Epstein is the saddest and least interesting figure in the entire Beatles saga.
Yet despite the occasional moments of chemistry in the cast, this is only a partly told story, one of those shows which, the more you think about it, the less satisfying it feels.
But the whole enterprise lacks the throb of the music that underpins all this sex, drugs and excitement.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this Brian Epstein biodrama, finding it a heartfelt but superficial exploration of the Beatles' manager. While the focus on an overlooked figure intrigues, most fault the speculative romance and absence of actual Beatles music.
